articles.title: Gulf shipping crisis deepens as Iran reports tanker fires, Houthis hit Saudi oil facilities - The News Pakistan
articles.summary: Gulf shipping crisis deepens as Iran reports tanker fires, Houthis hit Saudi oil facilities  The News Pakistan
articles.full_text:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said four oil tankers had caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, while separate maritime security reports pointed to further attacks on commercial shipping, as the widening conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel continued to threaten critical energy infrastructure across the Gulf.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the tankers had attempted to navigate routes it described as unauthorised. In its latest statement, it reported that a fourth vessel, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil, had struck a naval mine, suffered a powerful explosion and caught fire, Iranian state media reported on Friday.
An earlier IRGC Navy statement had reported that another tanker carrying two million barrels of crude had struck a mine.
Reuters could not independently verify the Iranian military's account.
Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said it had received a report that a crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while completing an outbound transit through the strait.
In an earlier incident report, UKMTO said a vessel had been hit on its port side about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran's Lavan Island, triggering a fire on board. Its crew were reported safe, with no environmental impact.
It was not immediately clear whether the vessels involved in the UKMTO reports were among the four tankers cited by Iran.
In a separate report on Friday, Reuters said UKMTO had reported a tanker being struck by explosive devices attached to a small boat, in what maritime sources described as the first known successful limpet-mine attack in the waterway since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February.
The incidents underline the growing dangers to commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage connecting the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea through which around a fifth of the world's oil supplies passed before the conflict.
Iranian state media also reported that its forces had downed and captured an MQM-170 US drone over Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate US military response to that claim, which Reuters could not independently verify.
Tehran also said it had destroyed an unmanned US vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
However, the US military's Central Command rejected the claim, saying all American unmanned surface vessels in the Middle East were accounted for, including a squadron of advanced sea drones patrolling the waterway.
The latest maritime incidents come amid heightened tensions following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February and subsequent Iranian attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure across the region.
Reuters reported earlier this month that Iran had shifted towards intensifying attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, seeking to keep oil prices elevated and increase pressure on Washington.
At least seven incidents involving tankers were reported during a week in early October, according to maritime intelligence service Marisks. The incidents included attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, raising concerns over the security of energy exports from the Gulf.
The maritime security crisis has coincided with a renewed Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia, further widening the conflict's geographical reach.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked several Saudi energy facilities, including the Ras Tanura refinery, the Rabigh refinery and a production facility at Abqaiq owned by state oil giant Saudi Aramco.
A Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's western region.
The attacks followed repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, oil installations and other critical infrastructure this month, including an October 10 attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, according to Reuters.
The Houthis have also threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, warning civilians, workers and international shipping companies to stay away from sites they consider legitimate targets.
The renewed offensive has severely disrupted Saudi aviation. According to aviation analytics firm Cirium, 4,071 of 4,736 scheduled flights at Riyadh's airport, or 86%, were cancelled between October 8 and October 25.
More than 7,800 flights, accounting for 45% of scheduled departures across Saudi airports, were cancelled during the same period.
The United States on Friday confirmed that it had ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia, effective October 23, citing security risks from Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure.
The US embassy in Riyadh warned American citizens of possible further attacks, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions.
The fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has intensified in recent weeks, opening another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.
A truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition collapsed in July. The group subsequently declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, attacked Saudi vessels and the East-West pipeline, and seized Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Reuters.
The military escalation has continued despite diplomatic efforts involving regional powers to prevent the conflict from spreading further.
Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of coordinated efforts to reach an agreement between Washington and Tehran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country obtain medical supplies, following reports that Vance had written to Tehran's top security official in an effort to revive peace negotiations.
Iran has confirmed receiving Vance's letter but has yet to respond, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. Tehran has said Washington must meet its conditions for an agreement.
Earlier this week, Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials met Iranian leaders in Tehran and agreed to continue discussions, although the agenda and substance of the talks have not been disclosed.
Pakistan's military said on Friday it was "cautiously optimistic" about Islamabad's mediation efforts, following two visits to Tehran this month by Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin accompanied Munir during his latest visit.
The diplomatic engagement comes against the backdrop of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7, under which an attack on any signatory is to be treated as an attack on all.
Pakistan's military spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said the agreement did not rule out additional members, including Iran, although any expansion would require a decision by the signatories' political leadership.
The mounting security risks have added to concerns over global energy supplies, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining a critical chokepoint for crude oil and fuel shipments.
Oil prices rose more than 2% on Friday, settling at their highest levels since late April as traders weighed the possibility of further escalation and the risks to supplies from the Middle East.
Brent crude futures for December delivery settled $2.76 higher, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate rose $2.12, or 2.08%, to $104.12.
For October, Brent gained 13.6%, while WTI rose 15.2%.
The attacks have raised concerns about the ability of Gulf producers to maintain exports through both the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, particularly as Saudi Arabia faces renewed threats to its oil infrastructure and Red Sea shipping access.
Saudi crude exports nevertheless increased in October compared with September, according to two of three ship-tracking companies cited by Reuters, despite Iranian attacks on shipping and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi energy facilities.
With Washington and Tehran yet to reach an agreement, the combination of maritime attacks, renewed fighting in Yemen and threats to Gulf energy infrastructure continues to complicate diplomatic efforts to contain the eight-month-old conflict.

articles.title: Iran's Khamenei warns US against attacks, orders military buildup
articles.summary: Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned that any renewed U.S. or Israeli attack would trigger an immediate and geographically wider Iranian response, ordering the armed f...
articles.full_text:
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned that any renewed U.S. or Israeli attack would trigger an immediate and geographically wider Iranian response, ordering the armed forces to expand their target lists, strengthen intelligence capabilities and accelerate weapons production.
In a written message following a meeting with senior military commanders Saturday, Khamenei said Iran would determine the timing and conditions for ending any future conflict if its adversaries resumed military or terrorist attacks.
He ordered the armed forces to prepare an "immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response" to any threat, stressing that maintaining a high level of combat readiness was essential to deterring further aggression.
"Intelligent combat readiness for a powerful confrontation with enemies is a fundamental prerequisite for achieving maximum deterrence," he said.
Khamenei also instructed military commanders to update their target database to bring "all U.S. and Israeli assets, tangible and intangible," within striking range, signaling an effort to broaden Iran's potential targeting capabilities in the event of another confrontation.
The directives included strengthening military intelligence, developing domestic defense capabilities and adapting military doctrine and tactics to emerging threats. He also ordered increased production of ammunition and weapons for reconnaissance, logistical support and combat operations.
The meeting brought together senior military officials, including Maj. Gen. Abdollahi, chief of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces; Maj. Gen. Hatami, commander of the Iranian army; and Maj. Gen. Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The commanders briefed Khamenei on military readiness along the Persian Gulf coast, in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, as well as along the country's northwestern and southeastern borders.
They also reported a significant increase in the production of key ammunition and various weapons systems for reconnaissance, support and combat missions. Khamenei expressed satisfaction with the preparations and asked the commanders to convey his appreciation to military personnel, police officers, Basij forces, Defense Ministry employees and their families.
Beyond military preparations, the supreme leader stressed the importance of strengthening the armed forces' ideological and spiritual foundations while addressing the welfare needs of personnel.
He also described public support as a central element of Iran's deterrence strategy, portraying continued public gatherings across the country as an extension of the national solidarity displayed during the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War, which Tehran calls the Sacred Defense.
Khamenei praised the resilience of the so-called Resistance Front, referring to Iran-aligned groups across the region, and highlighted closer coordination among operational fronts as a factor in shaping a new political and security order in West Asia. He expressed hope that such cooperation would encourage greater unity among Muslim nations.
His latest instructions come amid continuing tensions following the U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran, which began Feb. 28 and killed then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several senior military commanders.
Iran retaliated with attacks against Israel and U.S. military assets across the Middle East, widening the confrontation and raising concerns about the security of regional shipping and energy supplies.
Although Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum in June following diplomatic efforts, disagreements over regional security arrangements and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz have kept tensions high.
The strategic waterway, through which a significant share of the world's oil shipments passes, has remained a major point of contention, with Iran maintaining pressure on maritime traffic as the U.S. sustains its military presence in the region and reported blockade measures affecting Iranian ports.
Regional diplomatic efforts, including mediation involving Qatar, have yet to produce a lasting resolution.
Iranian army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia reinforced Tehran's warnings Saturday, saying a renewed confrontation would spread beyond its previous geographical boundaries if U.S. President Donald Trump launched another military operation against Iran alongside Israel.
"If the U.S. president once again embarks on another military adventure in the region under pressure from and inducement by the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," Akraminia wrote on X.
"And the end of the conflict will not be in his (Trump's) hands," he added.
Accusing Washington of repeatedly undermining diplomatic efforts, Akraminia said the Iranian army was continuously strengthening its combat readiness and closely monitoring U.S. military movements across the region.
His remarks came as Tehran and Washington remained at odds over the terms of any lasting settlement, particularly security arrangements and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father earlier this year, has maintained a relatively low public profile since taking office amid the conflict. His previous warnings have focused on U.S. military bases in the region, the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's conditions for ending hostilities, including demands concerning sanctions, blockades and regional security.

articles.title: Syria considers joining Mecca defense pact
articles.summary: Syria is considering joining the Mecca Defence Alliance, a NATO-style security pact linking Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Saturday, si...
articles.full_text:
Syria is considering joining the Mecca Defence Alliance, a NATO-style security pact linking Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Saturday, signaling Damascus' interest in deeper regional security cooperation as it seeks to rebuild its military and strengthen diplomatic ties.
"Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria's entry into the Mecca alliance," al-Shaibani said during the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) Manama Dialogue in Bahrain.
His remarks indicate that Damascus is seriously examining membership, although no formal application or final decision has been announced.
The pact was signed Aug. 7 in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Its central provision considers an armed attack against one member an attack against all three, allowing them to invoke their collective right to self-defense under Article 51 of the U.N. Charter.
The agreement also provides for intelligence sharing, joint military exercises, counterterrorism coordination and defense-industrial cooperation, including potential joint production and technology transfers.
The alliance established a Strategic Political and Defence Committee to oversee its activities and a permanent secretariat in Riyadh. Pakistan's retired Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood was appointed its first secretary-general for a three-year term. Membership is open to other countries with the unanimous approval of the founding members.
The arrangement builds on a mutual defense agreement signed by Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in September 2025. Its implementation gained momentum in October, when renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi targets prompted an emergency meeting in Riyadh. The alliance agreed to rapidly deploy previously agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia as a collective defense measure.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have completed their ratification processes, while Türkiye's domestic approval process remains underway.
Damascus first publicly acknowledged its interest in the alliance in late August, when al-Shaibani visited Islamabad. The trip marked the first visit to Pakistan by a Syrian foreign minister in nearly two decades.
At the time, he confirmed that Syria had reviewed the agreement but stressed that no decision had been made. He described the three founding countries as important regional powers and highlighted Türkiye's role as a key partner in Syria's reconstruction and security.
The issue gained renewed attention following Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's Oct. 6 visit to Riyadh for talks with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, amid efforts to strengthen Syria's relations with Arab countries.
Reports suggesting Damascus could provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia were subsequently denied by Syrian officials, who stressed that any cooperation would take place through established bilateral channels.
Syria's interest comes as its transitional leadership works to restore state institutions following the collapse of Bashar Assad's rule. The government has prioritized rebuilding the armed forces, strengthening ties with neighboring countries and reintegrating into regional diplomatic and security structures.
Speaking in Bahrain, al-Shaibani portrayed Syria as a country seeking to move beyond years of instability and contribute to regional security. He also condemned Israeli military operations on Syrian territory, citing more than 1,000 incidents since late 2024, and called for a return to pre-December 2024 positions and the reactivation of the 1974 disengagement agreement between Syria and Israel.
Joining the alliance could give Syria access to intelligence sharing, military training and defense cooperation while providing a framework for collective security commitments.
For Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Syrian membership would extend the alliance's reach into the strategically important Levant. Türkiye already maintains extensive military and security cooperation with Damascus, including efforts to rebuild Syria's armed forces.
However, Syria's military remains in the process of reconstruction and integration after years of conflict. Establishing the operational capacity and military coordination required for meaningful participation could take considerable time.
Any accession would also require unanimous approval from the three founding members and careful management of Syria's relations with other regional powers, particularly Israel and Iran.
Other countries, including Bangladesh and potentially Egypt, have expressed varying levels of interest in the framework or related security cooperation.

articles.title: Obama, Trump trade Cheesecake Factory jabs in midterm campaign
articles.summary: Former President Barack Obama and President Donald Trump have turned the Cheesecake Factory into an unlikely point of contention in the final days of the midterm election campaign,...
articles.full_text:
Former President Barack Obama and President Donald Trump have turned the Cheesecake Factory into an unlikely point of contention in the final days of the midterm election campaign, trading jabs as voters prepare to decide control of Congress.
Obama took aim at Trump's gold-heavy White House renovations during an Oct. 24 campaign appearance in Ohio, mocking the president for making the residence look as though "Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."
The remark drew a sharp response from Trump this week, who launched into lengthy defenses of both his White House renovations and the restaurant chain.
The exchange is the latest unusual distraction in an increasingly colorful campaign. Trump has issued warnings about communism, commented on men's physiques and joked that the $5,000 payments he has pledged to Americans if Republicans retain control of Congress would barely cover a meal at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida.
Both men are trying to portray the opposing party as disconnected from voters' economic anxieties as Americans grapple with high prices, a central issue heading into Tuesday's election.
Campaigning for Democrats in Morrow, Georgia, on Wednesday, Obama said Trump and his supporters were focusing on his Cheesecake Factory remarks rather than inflation, hoping voters would not notice that their bills were rising and their lives were becoming more difficult.
"They mobilized a whole-of-government response to that joke, not to inflation, but to that joke," Obama said. "They don't have solutions to actual problems, so they'd rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory."
Responding to conservative critics who suggested his joke mocked the restaurant's customers, Obama said: "I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory?"
Trump seized on Obama's remarks during campaign stops in Texas and Mississippi.
"Every piece of lettuce he eats has to be perfect, and I'm not that choosy," Trump said in Corpus Christi, Texas, waving his arms as if shaping a lettuce leaf.
Trump accused Obama of elitism for mocking the restaurant chain, known for its extensive menu and eclectic decor, which can include Egyptian-style columns and palm trees. He also dismissed criticism of his White House renovations.
"For you to say it's a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president," Trump said in comments to reporters on Monday.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent joined the exchange Tuesday, eating a French dip cheeseburger at a Cheesecake Factory restaurant in Washington and saying "the Martha's Vineyard set" should give the chain a try. Obama owns a home on the upscale Massachusetts island.
The episode is the latest flare-up in a rivalry that dates to 2011, when Trump gained political prominence by falsely questioning whether Obama was born in the United States. Obama later mocked Trump during remarks at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner.
During this year's midterm campaign, Democrats have accused Trump of being out of touch with the concerns of ordinary Americans, while Trump has repeatedly played down rising gas prices since the war with Iran began.
Trump gave his opponents another opening this week when he discussed in Texas how Americans should spend the $5,000 checks he has proposed sending them if Republicans retain control of Congress.
"You could even come to Mar-a-Lago," Trump said. "The problem is that for $5,000 the most you'll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert."

articles.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government is open to formally apologizing for Britain's role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade but ruled out financial reparations...
articles.full_text:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government is open to formally apologizing for Britain's role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade but ruled out financial reparations, ahead of a Commonwealth summit where Caribbean and African leaders are expected to renew demands for historical justice.
In an article published Saturday in The Guardian, Burnham said Britain was prepared to begin a structured dialogue with countries and communities affected by slavery, acknowledging that its failure to confront the past had damaged relations within the Commonwealth.
"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery," he wrote. "By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function."
Burnham said listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state would be an important part of the proposed discussions, adding that he was open to such a step.
"The trans-Atlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people," he said, expressing sorrow and regret for the suffering of millions of enslaved Africans and acknowledging the lasting impact of slavery on the modern world.
However, the prime minister firmly rejected demands for Britain to pay reparations, arguing that people living in the country today should not be held financially responsible for historical crimes in which they had no personal involvement.
"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," he wrote.
His position sets the stage for potentially difficult discussions at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, scheduled for Nov. 1-4 in Antigua and Barbuda, where reparations are expected to feature prominently.
The trans-Atlantic slave trade saw at least 12.5 million Africans abducted and transported across the ocean between the 15th and 19th centuries, according to the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database. Britain transported an estimated 3.2 million of them, building considerable wealth through the forced labor of enslaved people in its colonies.
Britain passed legislation abolishing the slave trade in 1807 before outlawing slavery throughout most of its empire in 1833. Successive governments have traditionally emphasized the country's role in ending the trade, while avoiding a formal acknowledgment of its responsibility for the suffering and wealth generated by slavery.
Burnham said Britain needed to recognize both sides of that history, arguing that acknowledging its participation was essential to rebuilding trust with Commonwealth members.
The issue has gained renewed attention during King Charles III's Caribbean tour, which precedes the summit. The monarch has faced calls for Britain to apologize and pay reparations for its colonial past.
Speaking in Nassau, the capital of the Bahamas, on Tuesday, Charles acknowledged "the great suffering and injustices of the past," but stopped short of issuing an apology. As a constitutional monarch, he speaks on behalf of the elected government and has traditionally been bound by its position on the issue.
The king is due to address Commonwealth leaders during the meeting in St. John's, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda.
Caribbean nations have increasingly framed reparatory justice as a broader effort to address the lasting economic and social consequences of slavery. Their demands include debt relief, development financing, investment in education and health care, and assistance with climate resilience.
Burnham sought to redirect part of the discussion toward those present-day challenges, proposing a new debt-relief initiative to help vulnerable developing countries repay loans over longer periods and at lower interest rates.
He said he would work with other wealthy nations and investors to advance the proposal, with former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, a longtime advocate of debt relief for developing countries, expected to attend the Commonwealth gathering.
Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne welcomed Burnham's willingness to consider an apology and his proposals for practical assistance. However, he made clear that the Caribbean's position on reparations had not changed.
"The Caribbean's longstanding position on reparatory justice remains unchanged," Browne wrote in a Facebook post.
Burnham's remarks also come amid growing pressure within Britain to confront its colonial legacy. In 2020, protesters in Bristol pulled down a statue of Edward Colston, a 17th-century merchant and politician who played a prominent role in the Royal African Company, which transported thousands of enslaved Africans to English colonies in the Americas.
The incident intensified debate over how Britain commemorates figures who accumulated wealth through slavery.
Some institutions and families connected to the trade have already acknowledged their historical involvement and offered apologies or compensation. The Guardian's owner, for example, has previously apologized for the newspaper's historical links to slavery.

articles.title: Abuse survivors look to Pope Leo for accountability, lasting reform
articles.summary: As Pope Leo prepares for his return to South America, Peruvian abuse survivor Pedro Salinas reflects on the hope and lingering doubts surrounding the pontiff’s efforts to confront...
articles.full_text:
As Pope Leo prepares for his return to South America, Peruvian abuse survivor Pedro Salinas reflects on the hope and lingering doubts surrounding the pontiff’s efforts to confront sexual abuse within the Catholic Church.
For a decade, Salinas followed the Church’s investigation into Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, a Peru-founded Catholic movement he helped expose over allegations of sexual, physical and psychological abuse.
The effort culminated in the final days of Pope Francis’ papacy last year, when the Vatican dissolved the group and its affiliated branches.
“What was achieved, nobody, absolutely nobody, could even have imagined. It was inconceivable. But it happened,” said Salinas, 63, a journalist and former member whose reporting played a key role in bringing the allegations to light.
Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo, quietly supported survivors and advocates during his time as a bishop in Peru and later as a Vatican cardinal, Salinas said.
He attended meetings, helped gather information and maintained contact with those involved through WhatsApp and email.
“Without him, the needle didn't move,” Salinas said.
The first U.S.-born pope will travel through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 to 17, spending the final six days in Peru, where he arrived as a missionary in the 1980s and later became a citizen and served as bishop of Chiclayo. The Vatican said he will meet with clergy abuse survivors there, as he has done on other recent trips.
Survivors say they wonder whether Leo's approach in Peru, which they credit with helping bring about the rare step of dissolving a Catholic community, can translate into broader change across a Church where accountability remains uneven.
“What is lacking are bishops everywhere in the world committed to this issue,” Salinas said.
Peru is preparing for a tourism boom during Leo's visit. José Enrique Escardó, 56, president of a Peruvian survivors network, views the excitement from a different perspective.
While Escardó acknowledged that some survivors credit Leo with helping dissolve Sodalitium, he said the Church's actions have not delivered sufficient justice, accountability or reparations.
“Survivors have grown tired of being told things, of being promised things, but nothing being done,” Escardo said. “We feel more abandoned. We feel deceived.”
He wants survivors to have a role in shaping Church policy and believes reparations should include psychological care and education.
The Vatican did not respond to a request for comment.
Francis, the first Latin American pope, left a complicated legacy, survivors say.
Juan Carlos Cruz, a survivor whose case became central to Francis' 2018 reckoning with abuse in Chile, credits the former pope with introducing changes that included revisions to canon law, the removal of the pontifical secret, the Church's highest level of confidentiality, from abuse cases, and the introduction of Vos Estis Lux Mundi, a Vatican framework for addressing allegations of abuse or cover-ups involving bishops.
“We're still at the tip of the iceberg,” said Cruz, whom Francis appointed in 2021 to the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors. “The commission has been working for years on universal safeguarding guidelines, and those standards need to be applied around the world.”
Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of the watchdog group BishopAccountability.org, which tracks Catholic Church abuse allegations worldwide, called Vos Estis the most significant action Francis took on abuse. But she said the Vatican rarely makes clear whether an accused bishop's resignation represents punishment.
“The public is left in the dark,” she said.
Barrett Doyle said the Vatican has not released global disciplinary data comparable to figures it provided to a United Nations committee in 2014. Her group relies on public records, media reports and investigations by prosecutors, governments and commissions to track cases.
She wants Leo to make permanent removal from ministry the universal rule for priests found under canon law to have sexually abused children, extending worldwide a policy adopted by U.S. bishops in 2002.
“To say that no child molesters should be out to practice as priests is just such a no-brainer,” she said. “It's a step that Leo could take now.”
Vatican officials have previously cited the difficulty of creating a single abuse reporting law across all countries and argued that removing priests can put them beyond Church supervision.
Angela Walker, executive director of the U.S.-based Survivors Network of those Abused by Priests, said survivors increasingly turn to civil authorities because of the Church's “incredible failure” to police itself.
“There needs to be more transparency, more openness and more accountability,” she said. “I will believe it when I see it.”
In Mexico, survivors pressed the Vatican on clerical abuse decades before it became a defining crisis across Latin America. Among the most notorious cases was that of Marcial Maciel, the Mexican priest who founded the Legion of Christ order and whose accusers took their allegations to the Vatican in the 1990s. The Vatican ordered Maciel in 2006 to withdraw from public ministry. He died in 2008 without ever facing his accusers.
The scale of his abuse became clearer after his death. In 2019, the Legion reported that Maciel had abused at least 60 minors, among 175 instances of child abuse the order documented involving 33 priests over eight decades.
Jose de Jesus Barba Martin, 87, alleged that Maciel abused him while he was studying for the priesthood in the 1950s. He recalled survivors struggling to be heard by Church and state authorities in the late 1990s and said an appeal he sent to Pope John Paul II went unanswered.
Decades later, that experience has left him with little expectation that another appeal to Rome would bring change.
“The Church is made up of two types of men: good and bad, courageous and cowardly,” he said. “It will take a long time, and the issue will not be addressed under this pope nor the next.”
Alberto Athie, 72, a former Mexican priest who pursued clerical abuse cases from inside the Church before leaving the priesthood in 2003, sees Leo's visit as another opportunity to push for transparency.
pedr
“I do have hope,” he said. “But my hope fades just the same ... Things have to be fixed within the Church.”
Abuse survivor Sebastian Cuattromo said the Argentine Church should have been “at the international forefront” of confronting abuse under Argentine Pope Francis but fell short of what he had hoped to see.
“There is a major outstanding debt,” Cuattromo said.
Argentina's Episcopal Conference declined to comment.

articles.title: UN wraps up 3-decade-long mission in conflict-hit Somalia
articles.summary: The United Nations political mission in Somalia officially ended Saturday following a two-year transition, bringing to a close more than three decades of U.N. political and peacebu...
articles.full_text:
The United Nations political mission in Somalia officially ended Saturday following a two-year transition, bringing to a close more than three decades of U.N. political and peacebuilding operations in the East African country.
Established by the U.N. Security Council in 2013, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNSOM) supported Somali authorities in efforts to strengthen democratic governance, uphold the rule of law and rebuild state institutions after more than two decades of conflict involving militias, terrorist groups and criminal gangs.
The mission traces its origins to 1995, when the U.N. established the United Nations Political Office for Somalia (UNPOS).
In May 2024, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud requested the mission's closure ahead of the expiration of its mandate in October that year.
He later revised the request, proposing a two-year transition period to allow for an orderly handover.
During the transition, UNSOM was replaced by the U.N. Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS).
"Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia. Rather, it marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another," said Raisedon Zenenga, UNTMIS officer-in-charge and the U.N. secretary-general's deputy special representative for Somalia, in a statement.
"While significant challenges remain, the closure of UNTMIS comes after considerable progress by Somalia since the early years of international efforts to support the country's recovery," he added.
The mission's responsibilities have been transferred to Somali institutions or the U.N. country team.
The transition comes as Al-Qaeda-linked Al-Shabaab, which has fought the Somali government for two decades, continues to control large swaths of central Somalia despite a major international military campaign against the group.
The fight against Al-Shabaab faces growing pressure from international funding cuts, particularly after the United States withdrew all funding for a key U.N. logistics mission, raising questions about the future of military operations.
Somalia is scheduled to hold parliamentary and presidential elections next May, but persistent insecurity and disputes between the government and opposition threaten the electoral process.

articles.title: Bangladesh records deadliest dengue month as deaths reach 418
articles.summary: Bangladesh recorded its deadliest month of the year for dengue in October, with 173 deaths as health experts warned that the outbreak is likely to persist through November and may...
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh recorded its deadliest month of the year for dengue in October, with 173 deaths as health experts warned that the outbreak is likely to persist through November and may not ease significantly until December.
The country reported 418 dengue deaths and more than 133,000 hospital admissions between Jan. 1 and Oct. 30, according to Health Ministry data. October's toll surpassed September's 148 deaths, making it the deadliest month of 2026 so far.
The surge comes as Bangladesh is also struggling with the world's worst measles outbreak, which has killed more than 1,200 people, placing additional pressure on an already overstretched health care system.
Doctors said many dengue patients were arriving at hospitals only after developing serious complications, making treatment more difficult.
At the state-run Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital in Dhaka, 279 dengue patients were receiving treatment after 67 new admissions in a single day, hospital director Mirza Golam Sarwar said.
"We are getting many patients in shock. Their blood pressure sometimes is too low to measure, and their oxygen levels are dropping," he said.
Medicine specialist ABM Abdullah said repeat infections, coupled with delays in diagnosis and treatment, were contributing to the rise in severe cases and deaths.
People who have previously contracted dengue face a greater risk of serious illness if infected again, he said, urging residents to eliminate mosquito breeding sites and seek medical attention as soon as symptoms appear.
The danger of repeated infections is a growing concern for residents such as Dhaka's Faisal Ferdous, who has contracted dengue three times, in 2017, 2024 and again earlier this month.
"This time, both my wife and I needed hospital treatment," said Ferdous, who is now recovering at home.
He said the couple fell ill shortly after spending several days at a hospital where their 5-year-old son was receiving treatment for an unrelated illness.
"Every bout has been difficult. After getting it repeatedly, you become increasingly concerned about the risk of severe illness," he said.
Health experts have also warned that the circulation of all four dengue virus serotypes is contributing to more severe infections. People previously infected with one serotype can develop more serious complications when subsequently infected with another.
Bangladesh has yet to introduce a dengue vaccine, although authorities are considering vaccination as a longer-term measure to tackle the disease.
Despite the October surge, entomologist Kabirul Bashar of Jahangirnagar University said the monthly death toll was unlikely to continue rising at the same pace. However, he warned that dengue transmission would probably remain high through November.
"We may see some relief, but dengue is unlikely to disappear in November. Any decline is likely to be modest, with significant improvement unlikely before December," he said.
Bashar said mosquitoes would continue emerging from breeding sites created by earlier rainfall, allowing transmission to persist even as weather conditions become drier.
He also pointed to changing rainfall and humidity patterns, partly linked to climate change, which are extending mosquito breeding seasons and allowing Aedes mosquitoes, the primary carriers of dengue, to remain active for longer.
The prolonged transmission season, combined with repeat infections and mounting pressure on hospitals, means Bangladesh is unlikely to see a substantial improvement in its dengue situation before the end of the year.

articles.title: Gen Z-led protests sweep 34 German cities over rising living costs
articles.summary: More than 160,000 people are expected to take to the streets across Germany on Saturday as a youth-led protest movement calls for better education, lower living costs and an end to...
articles.full_text:
More than 160,000 people are expected to take to the streets across Germany on Saturday as a youth-led protest movement calls for better education, lower living costs and an end to compulsory military service, organizers say.
The demonstrations, planned in 34 cities including Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich, are part of a wider wave of Gen Z-led activism sweeping Europe this year, with young people increasingly challenging government policies and demanding greater economic and social opportunities.
Organized by the campaign group Gen Z regelt, which translates as "Gen Z takes charge," the protests come as many young Germans face mounting financial pressures and concerns about the quality of public services and education. The movement is also opposing plans for compulsory military service, calling instead for greater government investment in schools and universities.
The demonstrations follow months of youth-led unrest elsewhere in Europe. In Serbia, student activism helped bring about the removal of the country's long-time leader through the ballot box, while protests in France have escalated into episodes of rioting, looting and clashes with police.
German authorities expect Saturday's rallies to remain largely peaceful but have warned that extremist groups could attempt to exploit the demonstrations to advance their own agendas.
According to the federal Interior Ministry, parts of Germany's far-left extremist scene and some organizations linked to foreign extremist movements have joined efforts to mobilize support for the protests.
The warnings have prompted concerns about possible violence, particularly in major cities preparing for large crowds. The demonstrations also coincide with Halloween celebrations, adding to security preparations.
"We all have those images from France in our minds, looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers," said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse.
"France must not be held up as a model in this regard," he added.
In Berlin, businesses along the upscale Kurfürstendamm shopping boulevard have taken precautions ahead of the demonstrations, with some boarding up their windows and planning to close early amid fears of possible unrest.
Despite the security concerns, organizers say the demonstrations are primarily about the economic difficulties and uncertain prospects facing younger generations in Europe's largest economy.
Germany is struggling to restore economic growth while confronting mounting pressure on its pension system and public services as the postwar baby-boom generation retires and the working-age population declines.
Young protesters argue that the government is failing to address their concerns, leaving them to shoulder the consequences of spending cuts and rising living costs.
"The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us," said Steve, an 18-year-old scheduled to speak at a rally in Munich, addressing Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"We will continue to exercise our fundamental right to assemble until you stop ignoring us," he said.
However, questions have emerged over the movement's leadership and how representative it is of Germany's younger generation, given the involvement of a broad range of political and civil society groups.
The country's national umbrella organization for school students, BSK, has distanced itself from Gen Z regelt and announced plans to organize a separate nationwide day of protests on Nov. 20.
The organization stressed that its decision did not amount to a rejection of the concerns driving the demonstrations.
"We are distancing ourselves from 'Gen Z regelt,' but not from the students themselves, who have legitimate concerns," BSK Secretary-General Amy Kirchhoff said Thursday.
Some students, meanwhile, say they plan to participate because of problems affecting their daily education.
Sean Baker, a student at the Technical University of Berlin, said he would join Saturday's demonstrations to highlight the deteriorating condition of university buildings and facilities.
"When you go inside and enter the rooms, it looks like an abandoned building," he told Reuters. "Yet this is where we're expected to study on a regular basis."

articles.title: DRC Ebola outbreak kills over 5,000, raises fears of wider spread
articles.summary: Deaths from an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo have surpassed 5,000, with the disease continuing to spread despite containment efforts and cases being reported i...
articles.full_text:
Deaths from an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo have surpassed 5,000, with the disease continuing to spread despite containment efforts and cases being reported in other African countries, according to the latest government data released Saturday.
Figures from the Congolese Ministry of Health showed that 5,026 people have died among 10,351 confirmed and suspected cases, putting the fatality rate at nearly 50%. The rising death toll has heightened concerns among health experts over the authorities' ability to bring the outbreak under control.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, was declared in mid-May, catching health authorities off guard and presenting major challenges to efforts to contain its spread. Since then, the disease has continued to claim lives as infections have extended beyond Congo's borders.
It has become the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, surpassed only by the 2014-2016 West African epidemic, which killed approximately 11,000 people across several countries over two years.
"It is a very tragic milestone because it is just not a number," said Dr. Patrick Otim, a program area manager with the World Health Organization. "It is families and communities that have been devastated by this outbreak. The number also shows the severity of this outbreak."
A total of 2,788 people have recovered from the virus so far. The Bundibugyo virus has no known vaccine or specific treatment, but health workers provide supportive care based on patients' symptoms.
Since May, the disease has spread to 67 of the country's 178 health zones in eight of its 26 provinces. Fifty of the 67 affected health zones have active cases.
The virus has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly in Ituri and North Kivu provinces, which have recorded a combined 9,782 confirmed cases and 4,792 deaths.
Authorities are still struggling with contact tracing and testing, key components of efforts to curb the outbreak.
According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 80% of new cases are being detected outside monitored chains of transmission, meaning health authorities cannot trace the infections to previously identified contacts.
One-third of recorded deaths have involved people who died outside treatment centers before being tested for Ebola, WHO's Otim said. Health officials say these challenges contribute to community transmission beyond the immediate reach of health workers and make it harder to ensure patients receive appropriate care.
"These are people we never had opportunity to try to save, and it is one of the biggest concerns for us in this outbreak. How do we try to reach people early to get them to come to health facilities to get a fighting chance to survive?" Otim said.
The surge in infections in Congo comes amid a series of challenges that have hampered efforts to contain the outbreak.
Eastern Congo, where the outbreak is concentrated, is also the scene of conflict between government forces and several armed groups, most prominently the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group. An Islamist insurgency along the border with Uganda, where the Allied Democratic Forces carry out attacks, has also restricted the movement and reach of health workers.
Widespread distrust among local communities has further complicated the response, contributing to attacks on health workers and medical facilities. A nurse was killed while responding to an Ebola alert last week, and a politician from the ruling party was killed in September after advocating health measures on the radio.
Health workers have also staged multiple strikes, shutting down facilities treating infected people over prolonged delays in government payments.
On Friday, workers at an Ebola treatment center in Tchomia, Ituri province, stopped working to demand four months of unpaid wages. The center currently has five confirmed Ebola patients and 10 suspected cases under care.
"We are tired of requesting our salaries. If they want to pay us, they will. ... Today, being able to feed our families has become a real problem," Moise Mugenyi, one of the striking workers, told The Associated Press.
Dr. Justin Mukonkole, acting head of response operations in Ituri, said workers should be patient as the government addresses their demands.
Similar situations have unfolded in other health zones, including Beni in North Kivu province, where services at some treatment centers have ground to a halt. Alain Siwako, an elected public official in Beni, said cases were spiraling because of a lack of fuel and financial resources from the central government.
"Across Ituri and North Kivu, this outbreak is stretching everyone responding to it, including the communities themselves," said Rose Tchwenko, country director for the Democratic Republic of Congo at Prosper Global, formerly Mercy Corps.
In October, Kenya and Nigeria both confirmed Ebola cases. Kenya reported eight cases and two deaths, while Nigeria's only confirmed patient was evacuated to Switzerland.
The cases in Kenya and Nigeria, following an earlier outbreak in Uganda, made the latest epidemic the first recorded across three African regions and the continent's most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak.

articles.title: France on edge as Halloween protests threaten to reignite riots
articles.summary: France is deploying 70,000 police officers and gendarmes across the country as authorities brace for another weekend of protests and possible violence over rising living costs, det...
articles.full_text:
France is deploying 70,000 police officers and gendarmes across the country as authorities brace for another weekend of protests and possible violence over rising living costs, deteriorating public services and growing dissatisfaction with President Emmanuel Macron's government.
The nationwide demonstrations, scheduled for Saturday, coincide with Halloween and come amid fears of renewed rioting after two consecutive weekends of unrest left shops, businesses and public buildings damaged in cities across the country.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has warned that the demonstrations carry a high risk of violence, particularly after dark, and pledged a forceful response to anyone involved in disorder.
"Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble," Nunez said earlier this week, describing the situation as carrying "a very high risk" of unrest.
Authorities are also concerned that protesters could exploit Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez said existing legislation allows police to prohibit face coverings when there is a threat to public order.
The U.S. Embassy in France has advised American travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations and large gatherings are expected.
In Paris, authorities have imposed additional restrictions in an effort to prevent a repeat of the Oct. 17 violence, when rioters looted hundreds of shops and security forces struggled to contain the disorder.
Police have restricted union and Yellow Vest demonstrations to a route along the capital's outer boulevards, running from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton, keeping marches away from the city center and major shopping districts.
Unions and student organizations have challenged the restrictions in court, arguing against the limitations on their right to demonstrate. Macron said Monday that marches would be kept away from central shopping areas to protect businesses.
Police have also prohibited access to Place de la Republique and Les Halles, two locations affected by the previous unrest, between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m. on Saturday and Sunday.
A separate 9 p.m. curfew applies to unaccompanied minors around the Champs-Elysees. However, a Paris court suspended an earlier curfew imposed on minors, ruling that it seriously and unlawfully infringed on freedom of movement.
The protests began in late September, initially driven by high school students angered by deteriorating school facilities, overcrowded classrooms and an admissions system they consider unfair. The movement has since expanded into a broader campaign against the rising cost of living, inadequate public services and government policies.
Trade unions and supporters of the resurgent Yellow Vest movement have joined the demonstrations, adding pressure on Macron's minority government as it negotiates the 2027 budget.
With public debt approaching 120% of economic output and borrowing costs rising, the government faces mounting pressure to reduce spending, leaving limited room to accommodate demands for greater investment in education and financial relief for households.
Authorities counted approximately 550,000 demonstrators nationwide on Oct. 17, when widespread looting accompanied the protests. Attendance fell to about 410,000 the following Saturday, when demonstrations were largely peaceful, although police made more than 1,300 arrests.
Government promises to improve education and ease fuel costs have done little to contain public anger.
"When I was little, I was told young people were the future," said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student from Nogent-sur-Marne, outside Paris, who planned to attend his third consecutive weekend of demonstrations.
"Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing."
The French protests have inspired youth-led demonstrations elsewhere in Europe, with rallies planned in more than 30 German cities on Saturday.
A youth initiative called Gen Z regelt, roughly translated as "Gen Z's got this," has called for demonstrations in Germany to demand improvements in education and health care, climate protection and more affordable living conditions, while opposing any return of compulsory military service.
Organizers said more than 140,000 people had registered their support online. Berlin police expected approximately 10,000 demonstrators to gather near the Brandenburg Gate.
Some businesses along Berlin's Kurfuerstendamm shopping boulevard have boarded up their windows in anticipation of possible unrest, although authorities said they had no specific information indicating planned violence.
In Spain, Catalan police prepared their highest level of alert in Barcelona after an anonymous network on TikTok known as Blocus called for further gatherings. Clashes during demonstrations the previous Saturday resulted in approximately 130 arrests, most involving minors.
Italian police also remained on alert following confrontations in Milan, Turin and Bologna, while calls for demonstrations circulated on social media in Belgium, the Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal.
The growing unrest comes as France faces mounting economic and political pressure. Figures released Friday showed the economy contracted in the third quarter, adding to concerns over the impact of prolonged instability.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates that retailers have suffered more than 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion) in losses. Other estimates put the overall economic damage at twice that amount when uninsured property damage and lost business revenue are included.
In Paris, the approaching Christmas shopping season has brought an unusual contrast to the capital's main commercial avenues, where festive lights illuminate streets lined with boarded-up windows and security grilles.
Luxury retailers, including Hermes, Louis Vuitton and Burberry, were among the businesses targeted during previous outbreaks of violence.
The government is also pursuing legislation that would make rioters financially responsible for damage caused either individually or by groups they are considered to belong to, with penalties reaching 10,000 euros.
